focus.statement: But it’s been my observation that the Greens—the economies that they admire are all in the Third World.
focus.explanation: A question about wages and employment law was before him; this engages no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome — it is entirely a characterisation of another party's supposed tastes. Classic content-free party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So whether it’s one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work. However, it is our intention as the Government, the moment someone is no longer able to work, to be on their case to get them back into work. So the consequences that that member’s talking about simply will not happen.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure at issue — 90-day trial periods and the trial length — and states the Government's intended operational response. On-policy, whatever the quality of the inference.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And whilst I’m at it, they left this country’s fuel supply in a desperate circumstance when they wound back Marsden Point. We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness, and Megan Woods is the person who never acted in international interests—just allowed the refinery that is so critical to this country in an emergency to be not operating any longer.
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision (the closure of the Marsden Point refinery), a named consequence (fuel supply resilience) and a timeframe (three days). This is scrutiny of a concrete policy outcome, not generalised party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won’t have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don’t just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them.
focus.explanation: A question about fuel and food costs was live; strip out the contrast between 'us' and 'that member' and no policy, figure or mechanism remains. Purely about which side keeps promises.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he stand by his decision to use parliamentary urgency to push through legislation that will increase unemployment and insecure working conditions, while reducing wages, when people are trying to survive a cost of living crisis and put more kai on the table for Christmas?
focus.explanation: Names a specific procedural decision (use of urgency), the legislation it carried, and the outcomes she says follow. This is scrutiny of a named government action, not tribalism, even though the framing is sharp.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But it’s been my observation that the Greens—the economies that they admire are all in the Third World.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the Greens as a party but lands on no individual — no attack on any person's character, competence or worth. The tribalism is Focus's problem, not Civility's.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, no, no. On the marae, Megan, you keep quiet. You do. Willie knows that; he keeps quiet too. You don’t shout out like some bunch of clowns at university.
civility.explanation: Directly personal: names two members, instructs one to 'keep quiet' by appeal to her place on a marae, and likens them to 'clowns'. This is contempt for the members rather than criticism of anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And whilst I’m at it, they left this country’s fuel supply in a desperate circumstance when they wound back Marsden Point. We could be closed down within three days because of their short-sightedness, and Megan Woods is the person who never acted in international interests—just allowed the refinery that is so critical to this country in an emergency to be not operating any longer.
civility.explanation: Turns from the decision to the person: says of a named member that she 'never acted in international interests', an imputation about her judgement and motives rather than about the policy. Pointed criticism of the refinery decision alone would have scored near 1.0.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, you are going to hold us to that—you won’t have to hold us to that because unlike that member, we keep our promises. We don’t just make them and break them one after the other; we keep them.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a specific member — that he makes and breaks promises 'one after the other'. Short of a direct insult but no longer civil under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just following on from the speaker who has resumed his seat, the reality is that there was a slight delay in the translation, reflective of the rudimentary nature of the Māori language and my ability to make it sound more sophisticated in English.
civility.explanation: A sneer delivered in a serious exchange about members' ability to be answered in te reo — disparages the language others in the House were using while flattering his own facility with English. Mockery aimed at the members raising the issue rather than engagement with their point.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, first of all, the integrity of the person answering this question on the subject of incomes and wages is that that threshold was set in the previous Government, not by Labour or the Greens but by New Zealand First.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the minimum wage threshold in place was set during the 2017-2020 government at the instigation of New Zealand First rather than Labour or the Greens.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2017 Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement text and contemporaneous Cabinet/MBIE minimum wage review papers; true if the minimum wage increase pathway is recorded as a New Zealand First coalition demand, false if it originated as Labour policy or Green policy with no NZ First provenance.

veracity.statement: That is the purpose and the focus of this Government—that with the reforms that are going to go ahead, running a far more successful economy, and ensuring that no one is left out in housing, education, and health, and in terms of infrastructure access, then people will be uplifted; not like the disaster we had, where there were all those tens and tens and tens of thousands utterly forgotten, and the homeless went up by 35 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantum — a 35 percent increase in homelessness — over the term of the preceding government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ severe housing deprivation estimates and MSD emergency housing/public housing register figures for 2017 compared with 2023; true if the relevant homelessness measure rose by approximately 35 percent over that period, false if the rise is materially different or the measure fell.

veracity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms' overall hiring, and that they instead reduced dismissal costs and made dismissal without cause easier.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 Motu/Treasury-commissioned study on the employment effects of the 90-day trial period; true if it reports no statistically significant increase in overall firm hiring attributable to trial periods, false if it reports a positive hiring effect or if no such Treasury-commissioned 2016 study exists.

veracity.statement: I’m advised that the 1:480 ratio was never finalised, nor was it funded adequately by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things about the police-to-population ratio referenced in the question: that it was never finalised as a commitment, and that it was not adequately funded by the preceding government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police and Treasury Budget documents and Cabinet papers from 2017-2023 referring to the 1:480 police-to-population ratio; true if no finalised ratio commitment and no matching appropriation can be located, false if a formalised 1:480 target with corresponding funding appears in those records.

veracity.statement: Well, in the police, numbers matter, and we’re committed to the coalition agreement that we have with New Zealand First. They delivered 1,800 additional police officers, and they’re now committed to an additional 500.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand First delivered 1,800 additional police officers during its time in the previous coalition government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police annual reports and constabulary FTE headcount series for 2017-2020/21 against the 1,800 additional officers commitment in the 2017 coalition agreement; true if the net increase in constabulary officers reached approximately 1,800, false if the net increase fell materially short.

rigor.statement: So whether it’s one month, two months, or three months, the fact of the matter is that the sound connection of those two will work. However, it is our intention as the Government, the moment someone is no longer able to work, to be on their case to get them back into work. So the consequences that that member’s talking about simply will not happen.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the premise offered is that a willing business and a willing worker produce employment, and the added premise is a case-management intention. Neither bears on the specific claim of disproportionate harm to young Māori workers, yet the conclusion asserted is that those consequences 'simply will not happen'. Nothing connects the premises to that denial.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So those pricings should go down.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that petrol prices will fall as a consequence of removing the fuel charging he describes as unfairly imposed by the previous government.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE weekly retail petrol price monitoring; true if the pump price in the affected region falls by approximately the removed levy amount following its removal, false if prices do not fall relative to the pre-removal level absent an offsetting international price move.

specificity.statement: Why is this Government planning to bring back 90-day trials, which will disproportionately punish tangata whenua, particularly rangatahi trying to get their foot in the door of the job market, when the research commissioned by the Treasury in 2016 found no evidence that trial periods increased firms’ overall hiring but instead just make it easier for firms to sack people without cause and with fewer dismissal costs?
specificity.explanation: Names the policy (90-day trial periods), the commissioning agency and year of the evidence (Treasury, 2016), the finding relied on, and the group affected. Someone could go and check every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why is law and order so important to me? Because people just want to feel safe—it’s as simple as that. When order becomes disorder, grandparents stop going out for grocery shopping, parents don’t let their kids walk home from school, and dairy owners have to serve people from within cages.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the premise (people want to feel safe) plus illustrative consequences is offered to support the conclusion that law and order matters. The link is coherent, but the supporting material is vivid illustration rather than evidence — an appeal to imagined anecdote, so the conclusion is only loosely carried.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We often hear that education is the key to breaking the cycles of poverty, unemployment, and crime, but I ask the House: why is education the common denominator? To me, it’s because if our people cannot read and write to begin with, they risk being shut out from society and the world.
rigor.explanation: Advances a mechanism (illiteracy leads to exclusion) to explain why education breaks cycles of poverty and crime. The mechanism plausibly supports the conclusion, but it is asserted rather than evidenced, and exclusion from society is a large step from illiteracy without anything offered to bridge it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While I strongly commend the traditional school systems, I also place merit in alternative school programmes and alternative education programmes and charter schools, because not every child learns the same way.
rigor.explanation: The premise (children learn differently) supports having varied provision in general, but does not reach the specific conclusion that charter schools in particular have merit — a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I want to make something very clear to my Māori brothers and sisters: if I felt that the National Party was racist, I would not be part of the National Party.
rigor.explanation: The implied conclusion — that National is not racist — rests entirely on the speaker's own membership and personal judgement. That is an appeal to personal testimony/authority; nothing independent of the speaker's own view is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our police should always be given the powers and resources they need to do the job they do best: keeping us safe.
specificity.explanation: A general commitment with no named power, no resource figure, no mechanism and no timeframe — 'the powers and resources they need' is self-defining and cannot be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Social investment in housing: when I worked at Te Mahia Community Village, a transitional housing facility in Takanini, I saw the significant drop in antisocial behaviour when social wraparound services are partnered with housing providers.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific facility and a specific intervention model (wraparound services partnered with housing providers), which gives it checkable anchors, but the claimed effect is 'a significant drop' with no figure, period or measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Takanini is enriched, with over 50 percent of its residents born overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than half of the residents of the Takanini electorate were born outside New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census birthplace data for the Takanini general electorate: true if the overseas-born share exceeds 50%, false if it is materially below.

veracity.statement: You ran the campaign the way you wanted, and in Takanini, I’m proud that we achieved the highest swing of the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Takanini campaign produced the largest swing of any electorate at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election results compared against 2020 results on the same boundaries: true if Takanini records the largest swing (party or candidate vote, on the basis the speaker's party used) of any electorate, false if another electorate's swing was larger.

veracity.statement: A fifth the size of New Zealand, Lebanon gave me my parents, John Hanna Fahd Rahme and Dalida Watfa Habib Rahme.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a size comparison between Lebanon and New Zealand — that Lebanon is one fifth New Zealand's size.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Land-area figures for Lebanon (~10,450 km2) and New Zealand (~268,000 km2) from CIA World Factbook / Stats NZ: true if Lebanon is approximately one fifth of New Zealand's area, false if the ratio is materially different. If read as population, UN/Stats NZ population estimates for 2024.

veracity.statement: Their own advice says so: the Department of Internal Affairs has on their own website, even today, advice that criticises the analysis that the Government has based their policy decisions on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that material published on the Department of Internal Affairs website as at 13 February 2024 criticises the analysis underpinning the Government's Local Water Done Well policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documents published on dia.govt.nz as at February 2024 (departmental advice, briefings, regulatory impact statements on water services reform): true if DIA-published material contains criticism of the analysis relied on for the Government's water policy; false if no such published material exists.

veracity.statement: Now, I live in Wairarapa, and in South Wairarapa that council has had no choice but to increase rates by 20 percent for two years in a row, and that doesn’t account for water services.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that South Wairarapa District Council raised rates by approximately 20 percent in each of two consecutive years, excluding water services costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: South Wairarapa District Council annual plans / long-term plan rates resolutions for the two financial years preceding February 2024: true if average rates increases of about 20% were adopted in both years, false if materially lower or if only one year reached that level.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister today was asked by Newshub about his numbers to justify their predictions. He walked away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 13 February 2024 the Prime Minister was questioned by Newshub about the figures underlying the Government's water policy claims and declined to answer, walking away.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Newshub broadcast/online footage and transcripts from 13 February 2024: true if the Prime Minister is shown being asked about the water policy numbers and leaving without answering; false if no such exchange occurred or he answered the question.

veracity.statement: What they are repealing, and what the members of the National, ACT, and New Zealand First parties are about to vote to do, is repeal the affordable water reforms—the reforms that the Government’s own advice shows would save ratepayers thousands a year by 2051.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice held by the Government projects savings to ratepayers of thousands of dollars per year by 2051 under the affordable water reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA / WICS modelling published with the Water Services Entities legislation: true if the official household cost projections show a saving of the order of thousands of dollars per household per year by 2051 relative to the status quo; false if the projections show materially smaller savings or no saving.

rigor.statement: They campaigned on the basis of having council control, council ownership, and balance sheet separation. And that is dishonest, because you can’t do them all—the advice says so.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference — the three campaign commitments are said to be mutually incompatible, therefore promising all three was dishonest — but the incompatibility rests entirely on an unnamed 'the advice', an appeal to unspecified authority, and the step from incompatible-promises to dishonesty assumes intent without supporting it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know because I sat down in front of every single rural and provincial council in the country and looked them in the eye and walked them through what it was we were trying to do, and they got it.
rigor.explanation: Supports the claim about why councils opposed the earlier reforms purely by appeal to the speaker's own anecdotal experience and personal authority; no council submission, survey or record is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There will be councils that want to join with others but can’t because those others don’t want to, because why on earth would they voluntarily agree to sign up to take on the debt and the burden that the other council brings?
rigor.explanation: A genuine mechanism argument: voluntary aggregation gives low-debt councils no incentive to absorb a high-debt partner's liabilities, so some councils will be unable to find partners. The inference follows, though it is put as a rhetorical question and assumes debt is the only consideration in amalgamation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have been asking the National Party to provide numbers to back up their claims right from when they first announced this policy 12 months ago and they have refused every single time, and now they’re in Government and they’re refusing again because they know it doesn’t stack up.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the numbers do not stack up and that ministers know it — is inferred solely from the absence of a released costing. Argument from absence of evidence, compounded by an unsupported claim about the opponents' private knowledge.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This won’t work, and I think deep down they know it but they don’t care. They don’t care because this gets this issue off the table.
focus.explanation: Contains a bare policy verdict ('this won't work') but the weight of the statement is about the other side's private motives and indifference rather than any named mechanism, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have been asking the National Party to provide numbers to back up their claims right from when they first announced this policy 12 months ago and they have refused every single time, and now they’re in Government and they’re refusing again because they know it doesn’t stack up.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names the specific policy, the specific thing sought (the costings behind the claims) and the specific failure to supply it over a stated period. This is holding the government to account on a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It is not unfeasible to say that there will be some councils that go bankrupt without a financial guarantee that this Government promised them when they were campaigning.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that one or more New Zealand territorial authorities will become insolvent in the absence of a Crown financial guarantee for water services.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: DIA / Office of the Auditor-General records and Local Government Act intervention notices: true if at least one territorial authority is declared insolvent, defaults on debt, or is placed under Crown management/commissioners for financial failure; false if no council reaches that state.

divination.statement: The West Coast is now left stranded. There is no way that Canterbury will join them—no one will.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that no Canterbury council — and no council at all outside the region — will enter a joint water services entity with the West Coast councils under the replacement regime.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Water services delivery plans accepted by DIA and the constitution documents of any joint water services council-controlled organisation: true if no Canterbury (or other out-of-region) council joins a West Coast joint entity; false if any does.

specificity.statement: Now, I live in Wairarapa, and in South Wairarapa that council has had no choice but to increase rates by 20 percent for two years in a row, and that doesn’t account for water services.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific council, a specific percentage increase and a specific duration, and expressly carves out water services — fully checkable against the council's annual plans.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What they are repealing, and what the members of the National, ACT, and New Zealand First parties are about to vote to do, is repeal the affordable water reforms—the reforms that the Government’s own advice shows would save ratepayers thousands a year by 2051.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure being repealed, the parties voting for it, an order-of-magnitude saving and a horizon year; checkable against the reform's published modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Prime Minister fronts up on any topic and on any question and he does so, on most parts, with a smile, although the smile’s not as wide as it once was these days, I might say.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe about the Prime Minister's demeanour rather than his policy — mocking in tone and directed at the man, though mild and delivered alongside a concession that he usually fronts up.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So they’re not concerned about “tough on crime”. They’re concerned about removing the ability to access what only the rich are left to be able to access. So how is that for some hypocritical action?
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the bill — that section 27 reports remain permissible but the funding for access is removed — and names who is affected. Party framing ('hypocritical') is present but the policy point carries the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Shame on them for trying to exploit rape—because using this racist legislation is trying to exploit rape and sexual violence.
focus.explanation: The legislation is named, but the content is almost entirely an attribution of motive to the other side rather than engagement with what the measure does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wish those members would roll their eyes in front of victims.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or outcome is named — it is entirely about how the members opposite are behaving.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So they’re not concerned about “tough on crime”. They’re concerned about removing the ability to access what only the rich are left to be able to access. So how is that for some hypocritical action?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: reports remain available, so the change bites on access rather than on the availability of reports. The leap from that to an imputed motive ('not concerned about tough on crime') is a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Not once, in three years of sitting with victims, as a Minister, have I heard them ask to remove these cultural reports. Not once.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal anecdote and absence of evidence: the speaker's own unrepresentative sample of conversations is offered as showing what victims collectively want. The conclusion outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know the power, in my very short time at the criminal bar, of actually having an employer turn up and speak on behalf of an offender and actually talk about how they can help that person actually stop their reoffending.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: his own brief experience at the bar is offered as ground for concluding that unfunded, informal advocacy will adequately substitute for funded reports. Nothing connects the anecdote to the general case.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can assure the House that I have held the victims after being raped, I have nursed the children who have been beaten, I have looked into the victim’s eyes, and I have retained a faith in the judiciary and the justice system to act appropriately.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal experience and emotion: lived proximity to victims is offered as the ground for the conclusion that the justice system acts appropriately. The experience does not bear on whether the system does so.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the judiciary who will weigh up the value of the information presented to them and they will know the difference between a well-coiled-up report written by professionals using special-speak and those impassioned pleas that are given by those who have genuine concern and connection to the offenders and want to see the very best outcomes.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to the authority of the judiciary, resting on an assumed dichotomy between professional reports and sincere personal pleas. Nothing is offered to show judges discount professional reports or that the two categories are exclusive.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So they’re not concerned about “tough on crime”. They’re concerned about removing the ability to access what only the rich are left to be able to access. So how is that for some hypocritical action?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to Government members — that their stated concern is a pretence — which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure, though it stops short of a personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Shame on them for trying to exploit rape—because using this racist legislation is trying to exploit rape and sexual violence.
civility.explanation: Imputes a depraved motive — deliberate exploitation of rape — to those advancing the bill. Aimed at the Government collectively rather than a named individual, but well past robust criticism of the policy itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wish those members would roll their eyes in front of victims.
civility.explanation: Mocks opposing members' conduct in the chamber and imputes callousness toward victims; a jibe at the people opposite rather than at their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge the passion from other members of the House, but we do have a different response to how we want to deal with criminal justice in New Zealand, and we see this as a part of an overall plan that our parties have put together to deal with it.
civility.explanation: Responding immediately after a fiercely personal speech, he acknowledges opponents' sincerity and frames the disagreement as one of approach. No imputation of motive or attack on anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is for that reason that we do not need taxpayer funding to milk the system, as has been occurring, but we do need the recognition of true, concerned community members to advocate for those who need it at the time of sentencing to represent their concerns.
civility.explanation: 'Milk the system' imputes bad faith and profiteering to those preparing funded reports, and 'true, concerned' implies the others are not. Short of a direct personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also was the chief panellist on the Owen Glenn inquiry into domestic violence and child abuse.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker held the role of chief panellist on the Glenn Inquiry into Child Abuse and Domestic Violence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published records of the Glenn Inquiry (its 2014 report 'The People's Report' and contemporaneous media naming its panel) listing panel membership and who chaired/led the panel; true if Davidson is recorded as chief/lead panellist, false if she held no such role or only ordinary panel membership.

veracity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that legal aid expenditure on section 27 (cultural background) reports was about $40,000 in 2017 and about $7.7 million in the most recent financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services legal aid expenditure figures on section 27 cultural reports for 2016/17 and 2022/23 (as released in answers to written questions and Budget material); true if the two figures match within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The ability to put information before the court, as has been well discussed tonight, will still be available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that after the Legal Services Amendment Bill, offenders will still be able to place cultural-background information before a sentencing court; only the legal aid funding for professionally prepared reports is removed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Legal Services Amendment Bill as reported back, read against section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002; true if section 27's right to call or provide such information is left intact and only legal aid funding is amended, false if the bill also restricts what may be put before the court.

specificity.statement: The problem as we see it is quite clear: in 2017, section 27 reports were costing $40,000; last financial year, $7.7 million.
specificity.explanation: Two dated dollar figures for a named funding line — directly checkable against public spending records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is for that reason that we do not need taxpayer funding to milk the system, as has been occurring, but we do need the recognition of true, concerned community members to advocate for those who need it at the time of sentencing to represent their concerns.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding at issue and the sentencing stage, but offers no figure, threshold or mechanism for how community advocacy is to be secured — the 'how much' and 'how' are absent.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because it was recognised that smoking and cigarettes were harmful, we moved towards an environment which was less and less smoky and, actually, fun fact, it wasn’t until 2016—2016—that the entire premises of Parliament finally became entirely smoke-free, including our lawn.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Parliament's entire premises, including the grounds/lawn, only became completely smoke-free in 2016.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service / Speaker's records and contemporaneous news reports on when the parliamentary precinct (buildings and grounds) was declared smokefree; true if the whole-precinct ban dates to 2016, false if it took effect in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: Well, it’s not the more New Zealanders who are going to be addicted for longer only filling up this Government’s coffers by an approximate $500 million per annum as a result of increased excise in tobacco tax; it’s going to be the tobacco industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal will increase Crown tobacco excise revenue by roughly $500 million a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Ministry of Health costings and Budget forecasts of tobacco excise revenue attributable to repealing the smokefree generation measures; true if the additional annual excise is around $500m, false if the official estimate is materially lower or higher (e.g. ~$250m/yr).

veracity.statement: There’s actually no cost-benefit analysis that sits alongside this legislation, I might add, which again leaves us with the question of why this is occurring under the urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill was introduced without any accompanying cost-benefit analysis.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's published documentation on legislation.govt.nz / Ministry of Health website — whether a regulatory impact statement or cost-benefit analysis was published with the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill; true if none exists, false if a CBA/RIS was published alongside it.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen it drop significantly over the past 12 years, from around 16 percent down to 8.6 percent last year, to 6.8 percent this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts daily smoking prevalence fell from about 16 percent twelve years ago to 8.6 percent in the previous year and 6.8 percent in the current year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence series (2011/12 through 2022/23); true if the three figures match the published rates within rounding, false if any is materially different (e.g. the prior-year rate is 8.0%, not 8.6%).

veracity.statement: I’d like to note that Action for Smokefree 2025 has said that the progress we’re making is unprecedented.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim that ASH NZ has characterised current progress on smoking reduction as unprecedented.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: ASH NZ public statements, media releases or survey commentary around 2023–2024; true if ASH described the decline in smoking rates as unprecedented, false if no such statement exists or ASH characterised progress as at risk from the repeal.

veracity.statement: Look, no regulations or programmes that were in place before the election have been stopped. That is the reality.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no smokefree regulation or programme that existed before the 2023 election has been discontinued by the Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act as enacted before October 2023 (denicotinisation, retailer reduction, smokefree generation) and the repeal bill's effect on them, plus Ministry of Health programme funding decisions; true if all pre-election regulations and programmes remain operative, false if any enacted measure or funded programme was repealed or halted.

rigor.statement: We’ve heard, time and again, from members of the Government that the reason that they feel entitled to push this and other legislation through under urgency is because they won an election—they won an election and they formed a Government, so therefore absolutely everything that they want to do, albeit that potentially only coming from one of the three coalition parties, is somehow able to be pushed through without any of the usual convention associated with the parliamentary process. So that kind of begs the question of whether they believe that authoritarian rule is “all g” simply because every three years we have a general election.
rigor.explanation: Engages a real process question (use of urgency and select committee bypass), but the inference from 'they invoke their electoral mandate to justify urgency' to 'they believe in authoritarian rule' is a slippery slope built on an inflated restatement of the Government's position.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we’ve kind of heard all of these weird arguments, which, on the one side, have said that this thing isn’t in effect yet, so therefore it’s not important, but yet we have a piece of repealing legislation that is being pushed through under urgency in order to repeal that thing which apparently is also not going to be effective but is also going to be far too effective.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine tension in the case for the bill (the measures are said to be both ineffective and urgent to remove), which is a valid form of argument; marked down because the two limbs are attributed loosely and could be held consistently (not yet in force vs. undesirable once in force), so the contradiction is partly constructed.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They want New Zealanders to forget. They are ripping off the band-aid really, really quickly in the hopes that this is swept under the rug amongst all of the other heinous things that they are doing under urgency and super-quickly with hopes that, into the future, New Zealanders forget it.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the Government's supposed motives and character rather than the measure; the only policy hook is the use of urgency, with no mechanism, figure or named consequence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We haven’t heard the Opposition give an intelligent reckoning with a second and third order of facts of prohibition of cigarettes on an emerging black market.
focus.explanation: Gestures at a real policy consideration (black-market effects of supply restriction), but the statement is framed as a complaint about the Opposition's performance rather than an engagement with the mechanism, cost or evidence.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They want New Zealanders to forget. They are ripping off the band-aid really, really quickly in the hopes that this is swept under the rug amongst all of the other heinous things that they are doing under urgency and super-quickly with hopes that, into the future, New Zealanders forget it.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — deliberate concealment from the public — to the Government collectively rather than engaging the substance, though no individual is insulted.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve seen it drop significantly over the past 12 years, from around 16 percent down to 8.6 percent last year, to 6.8 percent this year.
specificity.explanation: Three checkable prevalence figures with a stated timeframe; anyone could verify them against the published survey series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re supporting a package of initiatives to make sure we ensure a smoke-free goal of 2025.
specificity.explanation: An unnamed 'package of initiatives' with no components, funding, mechanism or timing — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: On the way we’re going, we will reach our goal of having the average under 5 percent by 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that national average smoking prevalence will be below 5 percent by 2025.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the year covering 2025; true if the national average is below 5.0%, false if it is 5.0% or above.

focus.statement: I am disappointed to hear that the rationale for not looking at sections 65C and 65J is because of the campaign approach, whereas it appears—unless the Minister advises the committee otherwise—that the same outcome for Aucklanders could none the less have been achieved by engaging those two sections of the Land Transport Management Act.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the legal mechanism at issue — named sections of the Land Transport Management Act and whether they could have delivered the same outcome. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My other question is in relation to clause 20, and this is about whether or not there are provisions, or any either flexibility or proposed leeway in the Minister’s mind in approaching this clause, or whether the provision provides for some flexibility around that, particularly around the payment of tax that might be required post-disbursal.
focus.explanation: Directly interrogates a numbered clause of the bill and the operational question of post-disbursal tax payment timeframes. Entirely on the measure, nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I will ask the fourth question as well, which is in relation to his answer about this benefiting all drivers. Has he had any advice about the impact of the regulation he’s proposing, given that it would seem that it would incentivise drivers to behave in different ways?
focus.explanation: Asks about the advice underpinning the measure and its behavioural incentive effects — entirely on the substance of the bill, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am disappointed to hear that the rationale for not looking at sections 65C and 65J is because of the campaign approach, whereas it appears—unless the Minister advises the committee otherwise—that the same outcome for Aucklanders could none the less have been achieved by engaging those two sections of the Land Transport Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statutory sections and the parent Act, though it does not spell out how those sections would have been used or what the resulting timing/cost would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, in my earlier contribution today, I’d indicated that I’d had a look at what one could get for $1.87 at a supermarket in Auckland, and what you could get is a 227-gram tin of chunky pineapple.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable illustration: a named dollar amount, a named product and its weight, tied to a named location.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the agency’s advice, in clause 18, all the advice that the New Zealand Transport Agency is required to provide the Minister currently, continues to be provided as the scheme is wound down. That relates to collection, auditing, administrating rebates, transferring net revenue, and monitoring revenue, cost, fuel prices, and volumes.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the agency and an itemised list of the advice functions carried over. Missing only the frequency the questioner asked about.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the question around passing on costs, there is a range of regulatory powers that MBIE have in terms of making sure that happens, and it’s very similar to what happened when the last Government reduced the fuel excise—those expectations remain.
specificity.explanation: Points to an agency and an analogous past episode, but names no particular power, monitoring mechanism or enforcement step — the 'how' the question asked for is not supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
specificity.explanation: Gives exact per-litre figures for both the tax and its GST component and the resulting saving mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to give the Minister a minute to consider my question, I will ask the second one, which is: who will benefit from those savings the most? And that should be read in the context of replacing some of the costs that were raised by the Government from the Auckland fuel tax with the $50 fee increase in drivers’ registrations of their vehicles.
specificity.explanation: Anchors the question in a named offsetting measure and a figure ($50 registration increase) against the Auckland fuel tax, though it quantifies neither the distributional effect nor the affected population.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This relates to the Minister’s own electorate, and I do think that the committee does deserve a response around the perception of conflicts of interest, given that the Minister is the member for Pakuranga and this is a project that would obviously be of huge benefit at the expense of other Aucklanders if this was to proceed.
civility.explanation: Raises a perception of conflict of interest against the Minister personally. It is framed as a request for a response rather than an accusation of corruption, but it edges past the policy onto the person's motives.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This goes back a long time, when Trevor Mallard was Minister of Education—so I’m afraid, Minister, this might have been before you were born, or perhaps not; it’s hard to tell.
civility.explanation: A light personal jibe at the Minister's youth. Not abusive and clearly good-humoured, but it is directed at the person rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I invite the—well, I’m interested in the Minister’s response, and my question to the Minister is whether he still stands by the cost of living argument when the departmental disclosure statement very clearly indicates that in some cases, motorists will be around $1.87 better off a week, and the real difference that that would actually make to entertain the cost of living pressures.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the departmental disclosure statement accompanying the bill states motorists will be about $1.87 a week better off in some cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill 2024; true if it gives a weekly household/motorist saving of approximately $1.87, false if no such figure appears or the stated figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: There are 14 projects that are suggested to be either retained or dispensed with under this bill, and each in their own right is going to have a huge impact either way on the communities in Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill/order before the committee covers 14 named projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule/order attached to the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill as introduced in March 2024; true if it lists 14 projects, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: There will be 10c plus the corresponding 1.5c a litre in GST that will be reduced from people’s fuel bills; they’ll benefit through this saving.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland regional fuel tax is 10c per litre and that the GST component on it is 1.5c per litre, so removal cuts 11.5c per litre from pump prices.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Land Transport Management (Regional Fuel Tax) rate for Auckland and the 15% GST arithmetic on it; true if the rate is 10c/litre and GST on that is ~1.5c/litre, false if either figure is materially different.

divination.statement: So it’s all very sensible stuff, which I’m sure the Opposition is very happy to support.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Opposition will support the bill (or at least these transitional provisions) at its subsequent stages.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill's remaining stages in 2024; true if Labour voted in favour, false if Labour voted against.

rigor.statement: Are we, in fact, passing on costs that would otherwise not have been borne by people like my 90-year-old father who drives his car very little but needs to register it every year, and subsidising those people like me who drive great distances because of their work and to get around Auckland?
rigor.explanation: The distributional inference genuinely follows: swapping a per-litre tax for a flat annual registration fee does shift incidence from high-mileage to low-mileage drivers. It leans partly on two personal anecdotes as illustration rather than on data, which is what keeps it short of the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because myself, I’m actually quite familiar with that process because I was a former journalist, actually, working here in Wellington for TV One News.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a biographical fact: that she previously worked as a journalist for TV One News (TVNZ) based in Wellington.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wedd's parliamentary/party biography, TVNZ employment or broadcast archive records; true if she was employed as a journalist for TVNZ's One News in Wellington, false if she held no such role.

veracity.statement: We want to make sure that small-business owners, who make up the majority of business owners in New Zealand, have the ability to enjoy the same kinds of protections that their big-business - owning counterparts have.
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual claim that small-business owners constitute the majority of business owners in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography statistics / MBIE small business data on the share of NZ enterprises that are small (commonly <20 employees); true if small businesses are a clear majority of enterprises, false if they are not.

veracity.statement: My colleagues made the point that the Institute of Directors have been asking for this for some time, that it is a stand-out thing that comes up for women in directors’ positions about why they would not become directors.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim that the Institute of Directors has been advocating for suppression of directors' residential addresses, and that address publication is a stand-out deterrent for women considering directorships.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Institute of Directors public statements, submissions or media releases on director address disclosure; true if the IoD has publicly sought this change, false if no such advocacy exists.

rigor.statement: So I suppose what I’m trying to get to here is that, you know, that information on the Companies Office website actually can be very beneficial in some cases.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single personal anecdote, but the conclusion drawn is only existential ('can be beneficial in some cases'), which one worked example does support. Modest gap between the evidence and any wider claim about the register's value.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view. That’s not available to the hairdressers and the tradies that Laura Trask spoke about tonight, and that’s why we should make this urgent change, even if there is further change coming later, which I welcome.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference from a stated asymmetry: large operators can already withhold addresses via limited partnerships, small operators cannot, therefore equalise. The conclusion tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If Labour and ACT can agree, surely we can agree that this is, indeed, sticking up for the little guy.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to consensus: cross-party agreement between two parties is offered as the reason the measure is right, which says nothing about the merits of the provision itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I hope members in all parties can listen to this debate and change their minds here and now, because there is nothing in this bill which would create harm, there is nothing in this bill which would put the directors in a worse position than they were before, and there’s certainly nothing in this bill that would put shareholders in a worse position than they were before.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a triple bare assertion of 'no harm' with nothing offered in support, and does not engage the harm the previous speaker had identified (loss of a means of tracing fraudulent directors).
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I suppose what I’m trying to get to here is that, you know, that information on the Companies Office website actually can be very beneficial in some cases.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the mechanism at issue — public disclosure on the Companies Office register — rather than about the sponsoring party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I hope members in all parties can listen to this debate and change their minds here and now, because there is nothing in this bill which would create harm, there is nothing in this bill which would put the directors in a worse position than they were before, and there’s certainly nothing in this bill that would put shareholders in a worse position than they were before.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the effects of the measure before the House on directors and shareholders; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There was obviously also another note there around the bill introducing a fee and perhaps that’s something that we also need to look at, and perhaps the lack of logic in some areas in terms of—giving the example around the shareholders and the directors and the discrepancy that we perhaps see there.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at two concerns (a fee, a director/shareholder discrepancy) without naming the fee amount, the clause, or what the discrepancy actually is; heavily hedged with 'perhaps'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They can use things that already enjoy the protections of limited liability, but still allow directors to not have their addresses published—things like limited partnerships which allow them to have all of their address details withheld from public view. That’s not available to the hairdressers and the tradies that Laura Trask spoke about tonight, and that’s why we should make this urgent change, even if there is further change coming later, which I welcome.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative mechanism (limited partnerships) and the exact protection it confers, though no figures, cost or timeframe are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Growth and more growth means jobs and more jobs, it means higher wages, and it means a better future for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-level assertion: no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy — nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve slashed the red tape, we’ve got rid of the bureaucracy, and we’ve been out in the world hustling for trade deals so we have better markets to send our good products to, and, wow, is that making a difference.
specificity.explanation: Claims a direction of travel but names no regulation removed, no trade agreement, no figure and no date — nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
specificity.explanation: A single named sector with a dollar figure and a period — directly checkable against export statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They have used the Investment Boost package of this Government, which enabled a 20 percent tax deduction along with depreciation.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the rate of the deduction and how it interacts with depreciation, applied to an identified local business.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the news today of the official cash rate dropping another 50 basis points and decreasing mortgage rates is welcome news for families struggling with mortgage repayments, but it is also welcome news for our growers, farmers, and businesses across Hawke’s Bay because it gives confidence and certainty and more money to invest in growing our economy and creating jobs, and this lifts wages for everyone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the official cash rate was cut by 50 basis points on the day of the speech (8 October 2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR decision released 8 October 2025: true if the cut announced was 50 basis points; false if it was a different size or no cut was made.

veracity.statement: A highlight in the last few weeks was visiting the Hastings Stortford Lodge saleyards, and it was amazing to see the farmer confidence back again, with record highs in farmer confidence because finally they have a Government that is backing them and allowing our farmers to do what they do best, and that is farm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that measured farmer confidence was at record highs around September/October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published farmer confidence surveys covering mid-late 2025 (Federated Farmers Farm Confidence Survey; Rabobank Rural Confidence Survey): true if a reading is the highest in the series' history, false if the readings are merely improved or below prior peaks.

veracity.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand apple export revenue never reached $1 billion in any year of the 2017-2023 Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MPI SOPI apple (and pear) export revenue by year 2017-2023: true if every year is below $1 billion, false if any year reached or exceeded it.

veracity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts horticulture export revenue of $8.5 billion in the current year, and that this is an all-time record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries horticulture export revenue for the year ending June 2025: true if approximately $8.5 billion and the highest in the series, false if materially different or below a previous year.

veracity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
veracity.explanation: Two linked assertions: roughly 360,000 people employed in the food and fibre sector, and that this is about 15 percent of New Zealand's total workforce.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI food and fibre sector employment figures and Stats NZ total employment: true if the headcount is near 360,000 and that headcount is close to 15% of total employment; false if the share is materially different (e.g. ~12-13%, the one-in-eight figure MPI commonly cites).

veracity.statement: They have used the Investment Boost package of this Government, which enabled a 20 percent tax deduction along with depreciation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's Investment Boost policy provides a 20 percent deduction on qualifying asset spending in addition to normal depreciation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Budget 2025 documentation of the Investment Boost: true if the scheme allows an immediate 20% deduction of a new asset's cost with the remaining 80% depreciated as usual, false if the rate or mechanism differs.

rigor.statement: Cattle were going out the gate for $3,500 each, and this is just phenomenal for the growth of our economy because it motivates more spending and puts more money back into the pockets of New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single observed sale price at one saleyard to a national economic conclusion; the inference from one anecdotal price to economy-wide spending and growth is unsupported by anything offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
focus.explanation: Names a specific sector and a specific export threshold as the point of comparison — accountability framing built on an identifiable outcome rather than generic party-bashing, though the framing is partisan.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In Hawke’s Bay alone, our region is set to add another thousand new jobs in agriculture and horticulture.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an increase of about 1,000 agriculture and horticulture jobs in the Hawke's Bay region — an outcome in the labour market, not a commitment by the speaker.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Infometrics regional employment data for Hawke's Bay in agriculture and horticulture: true if filled jobs in those industries rise by roughly 1,000 or more from the 2025 base, false if growth is materially smaller or negative.

specificity.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings. That continues to normalise violence.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact new provision (section 384KB) and the inserting clause (28), and identifies the specific mechanism objected to — permitted use of force in care settings. Checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures (28 of 138) tied to a named body of recommendations, though the remedy offered ('move a heck of a lot faster') carries no mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings. That continues to normalise violence.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: a named clause, its effect, and the alternative approach preferred. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
focus.explanation: Accountability for a named commitment against a counted outcome — the core scrutiny function. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By not recognising their harm and by minimising their harm, that is not the State taking accountability for its own violence; that is the State choosing to discriminate about who worthy survivors of violence are, and who deserves to have their violence recognised.
focus.explanation: Engages the design of the redress scheme — who is paid and on what basis — rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I leave that on the Hansard for that side of the House to have to live up to for decades—well, for ever now. It’s on the record. That’s what that side of the House has called for.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what 'that side of the House' is like and what it will be remembered for. Strip out the characterisation of the other side and no policy, figure or measure remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
focus.explanation: About the other side of the House and the quality of their contribution; no policy, clause or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of the 138 recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, only 28 have been completed or have progress initiated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown's published implementation reporting on the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (Whanaketia) recommendations as at October 2025 — true if the total number of recommendations is 138 and the number recorded as completed or with progress initiated is 28 (or materially the same), false if either figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: By not recognising their harm and by minimising their harm, that is not the State taking accountability for its own violence; that is the State choosing to discriminate about who worthy survivors of violence are, and who deserves to have their violence recognised.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference — a tiered redress entitlement implies a ranking of whose harm is recognised — but the leap from 'differentiated eligibility' to 'the State choosing to discriminate about who worthy survivors are' is asserted rather than shown; no reason is given to rule out non-discriminatory grounds for the tiering. A gap between what was offered and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: 'Rubbish that has been spouted' is dismissal by sneer rather than engagement — it characterises the previous speech contemptuously without addressing any part of it. Short of a direct personal insult, but past the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker
